question: If a company reports £500m of revenue, has it received £500m of cash?
model_answer_md:
No. Revenue is recognised when the company has **earned** it — delivered the goods or provided the service — not when the customer pays. That is the accrual principle, and it is the reason the cash flow statement exists.

If Kestrel sells £500m but customers still owe £50m at year end, that £50m sits on the balance sheet as **receivables**, not cash. The revenue is real; the cash simply has not arrived yet.

It runs the other way too. Cash collected before the work is done is not revenue — it is a liability, deferred revenue, until the company delivers.
key_points: Revenue is recognised when earned, not when paid
The unpaid portion sits in receivables on the balance sheet
Cash received before delivery is deferred revenue, a liability
This gap is exactly what the cash flow statement reconciles

follow_ups.question: Where does the gap show up?
follow_ups.answer_md: In two places. On the balance sheet as receivables, and on the cash flow statement as a working-capital movement: an increase in receivables is subtracted from net income, because the profit was booked but the cash was not collected.

follow_ups.question: Why does this matter for valuation?
follow_ups.answer_md: Because you are ultimately valuing cash, not accounting profit. A company growing revenue quickly while receivables grow faster is converting sales into cash more slowly, which consumes funding and can mask a deteriorating business. Revenue quality is one of the first things to test.

weak_answer_note: Answers simply 'yes' or confuses revenue with cash receipts. Also weak: mentioning receivables without explaining the accrual principle underneath.
